name: TMJ splint (orthotic)

lead: A TMJ splint is a removable acrylic appliance, usually custom-made by a dentist, that fits over the upper or lower teeth. In looksmaxxing circles the idea is that correcting jaw-joint imbalance can improve bite, jaw symmetry and facial balance.

Stabilization splints sit flat against the opposing teeth to relax the jaw muscles and spread bite forces. Repositioning splints hold the lower jaw in a different position, for example forward, to try to improve how the joint disc sits while worn. Studies focus on pain and joint function, and reviews describe modest evidence for hard stabilization splints in TMD pain and insufficient evidence on other points; appearance outcomes have not been researched.

paras: A dentist takes impressions and fits the splint, which is typically worn at night or for set periods, with follow-up adjustments. Use is generally considered reversible.

Partial-coverage splints can cause unwanted tooth movement, and orthodontic literature describes posterior open bites after repositioning splint therapy, which can need orthodontic work. Fit and use are monitored by the dentist.

angle.text: Users interested in jaw alignment discuss custom splints that stabilize or reposition the jaw joint, hoping for a more even bite and a more balanced face. Splints are used for TMJ disorders with modest evidence, and appearance outcomes have not been researched.

lead: A TMJ splint, also called an occlusal splint, bite splint or night guard, is a removable dental appliance molded to the upper or lower teeth. It is used to protect teeth, manage temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders, stabilize the joint, or alter the bite position.[1][2]

Two broad types are described. Stabilization (Michigan-type) splints sit flat against the opposing teeth to help relax jaw muscles. Repositioning splints hold the jaw in a different position, for example forward, in an attempt to improve the relationship of the joint disc.[1]

Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest evidence of benefit for hard stabilization splints in TMD pain, and insufficient evidence on other points.[2] No study found tested splints for facial appearance.
infobox: Heat-cured acrylic; soft materials for short-term use

paras: Heat-cured acrylic is the standard material and the most durable; soft acrylic, light-cured composite and vinyl are cheaper and faster to make but wear out faster. Splints may cover the full arch or part of it, and upper splints are more common than lower ones.[1]

A neuromuscular splint, made using low-frequency electrical stimulation to find a jaw position, is described as a temporary reversible diagnostic device.[1] Anterior repositioning splints are used in some practices for displaced joint discs.[3][4]

Proponents of the idea describe splints as a way to address jaw-joint imbalance that they believe may contribute to bite problems or jaw asymmetry. No published research tests this for facial appearance.

Evidence comes mostly from TMD treatment research rather than appearance. A 2010 review summarized by Wikipedia found good evidence of modest efficacy for hard stabilization splints in TMD pain when properly adjusted, while another review found insufficient evidence for or against them compared with other active treatments.[2] A meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia found not enough evidence that splints effectively treat sleep bruxism.[1]

Smaller clinical reports include a Russian study in which TMJ repositioning and functional rehabilitation was achieved in 87.2% of cases with splint plus hydraulic pressing, a minimally invasive combination.[5] Reports from a functional orthodontics practice describe splint therapy combined with open joint surgery in 60 patients (117 joints) who had not responded to earlier treatment.[6][7]
No studies found testing splints for changes in facial appearance.

Splints are generally considered reversible, though partial-coverage designs can cause unwanted tooth movement and other splint types carry a higher risk of adverse events.[2] Hard splints may need refitting in children because growth alters fit.[1]

Dental literature describes a difficult orthodontic problem in patients stabilized with an anterior repositioning splint: a posterior open bite can develop, with the front teeth meeting only in the splint-stabilized position, and orthodontic treatment may be proposed afterward.[3][4][8]

timeline.event: Rodney Lilyquist introduces a transparent acrylic splint, described by Wikipedia as an advance for athletes' mouth protection.[1]
Orthodontic papers describe treatment after anterior repositioning splint therapy.[3][4]
